title: Two Sum
candidateDescription: Given an array of integers nums and a target value, find two numbers that add up to the target and return their indices.
interviewerContext: Two Sum. Constraints: 2 <= nums.length <= 10^4, integers can be negative or positive, exactly one solution exists, cannot use the same element twice, return indices in any order. Optimal: O(n) hash map. Brute force: O(n^2). Edge cases: duplicates, negatives, large arrays.

hiddenTestCases.description: duplicate-value pair (tests same element can't be reused)
first valid pair among many candidates
target found by skipping the first element

followUps.prompt: Good. Now suppose the input array is guaranteed to be sorted in ascending order. Can you solve it in O(1) extra space instead of using a hash map?

title: Valid Anagram
candidateDescription: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram uses all original letters exactly once.
interviewerContext: Valid Anagram. s and t lengths up to 5 * 10^4, lowercase English letters. Optimal O(n) character counts or sort O(n log n). Edge: different lengths, empty strings, repeated chars.

followUps.prompt: Good. What if the strings could contain any Unicode characters — not just lowercase ASCII? Does your current solution still work, and is there anything you'd change?

title: Contains Duplicate
candidateDescription: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, otherwise return false.
interviewerContext: Contains Duplicate. Length up to 10^5, values roughly 32-bit range. Optimal O(n) set/hash. Sort O(n log n). Edge: two elements same, all unique, min/max ints.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
candidateDescription: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on day i. You may choose a single day to buy and a different later day to sell. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If no profit is possible, return 0.
interviewerContext: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock I. 1 <= prices.length <= 10^5, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4. Optimal: single pass tracking running minimum and best profit, O(n) time, O(1) space. Brute force: O(n^2) pairwise. Edge cases: monotonically decreasing (return 0), single day, all same price, large arrays. Common pitfall: buying and selling on the same day, or not enforcing buy < sell ordering.

hiddenTestCases.description: best window is in the middle, not at the start

followUps.prompt: Nice. Now suppose you can buy and sell as many times as you want, but you can only hold one share at a time. What's the maximum profit, and why?

title: Valid Parentheses
candidateDescription: Given a string s containing only the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. Brackets must close in the correct order: every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket of the same type and they are properly nested.
interviewerContext: Valid Parentheses. 1 <= s.length <= 10^4, only bracket chars. Optimal: O(n) stack — push openers, pop on matching closer, reject mismatch or empty pop. Edge: empty string is vacuously valid (LC says length>=1 but many candidates handle empty too), single closer, deeply nested, interleaved like ([)].

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
candidateDescription:
You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists, list1 and list2, represented as arrays of values in ascending order. Merge them into a single sorted linked list and return the merged list as an array of values.

Both input arrays are guaranteed to be sorted in non-decreasing order.
interviewerContext: Merge Two Sorted Lists. 0 <= length of each list <= 50. Values in [-100, 100]. Optimal: iterative two-pointer with a dummy head node, O(n+m) time, O(1) extra. Recursive solution is also clean. Edge: either list empty, both empty, fully disjoint ranges, duplicates across lists, single-node lists. Test harness exchanges value arrays — candidate writes the actual logic on ListNode using the provided helpers.

title: Maximum Subarray
candidateDescription: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum, and return its sum.
interviewerContext: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's algorithm). 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4. Optimal: Kadane's, O(n) time, O(1) space — running sum reset when it dips below 0. Divide and conquer is O(n log n). Edge: single element (positive or negative), all negatives (answer is the max single element), all positives, alternating signs. Common pitfall: initializing best to 0 — fails when all numbers are negative.

hiddenTestCases.description: single negative — answer is that element
best window is a single middle element
tiny array, choose the positive only
best window crosses a deep negative

title: Climbing Stairs
candidateDescription: You are climbing a staircase. It takes n steps to reach the top. Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
interviewerContext: Climbing Stairs. 1 <= n <= 45. f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2), f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2 — Fibonacci. Optimal: O(n) with two rolling vars, O(1) space. Memoized recursion also works. Closed form via Binet is O(1) but rarely expected. Edge: n=1, n=2, large n (n=45 → 1134903170).

hiddenTestCases.description: guards naive O(2^n) recursion against TLE
n=45 upper bound — guards against TLE on naive recursion

title: Reverse Linked List
candidateDescription: Given the head of a singly linked list, represented as an array of node values in order, reverse the list and return the reversed list as an array of values.
interviewerContext: Reverse Linked List. 0 <= length <= 5000. Optimal: O(n) iterative with prev / cur / next pointers, O(1) extra. Recursive is elegant but O(n) stack. Edge: empty list, single node, two nodes. Common pitfall: losing the next pointer before rewiring.

followUps.prompt: Solid. Now do it recursively. Walk me through the base case, the recursive step, and the stack depth.

title: Invert Binary Tree
candidateDescription:
Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree (swap every node's left and right subtree) and return its root.

The tree is provided as a level-order array using null for missing children (LeetCode encoding). Return the inverted tree in the same encoding.
interviewerContext: Invert Binary Tree. 0 <= nodes <= 100. Optimal: recursive swap, O(n) time, O(h) stack. BFS iterative also fine, O(n) time, O(w) queue. Edge: empty tree, single node, fully-left chain (tests stack depth on recursion), perfectly balanced. The famous 'Homebrew rejected for not being able to do this' problem.

title: Binary Search
candidateDescription: Given a sorted (ascending) array of integers nums and a target value, return the index of target if it is present in nums. Otherwise return -1. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime.
interviewerContext: Binary Search. 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, all unique. Optimal: classic O(log n) — careful with mid (low + (high-low)//2), inclusive vs half-open bounds, and termination. Edge: target at endpoints, single element, target absent (smaller than min / larger than max), even/odd length arrays. Common pitfall: integer overflow in other languages (not Python).

hiddenTestCases.description: target near end of even-length array

followUps.prompt: Good. Now suppose nums may contain duplicates — still sorted ascending. Return the leftmost index where nums[i] == target, or -1 if target is absent. Still O(log n). What changes in your loop when you find a match?

title: First Bad Version
candidateDescription:
You are a product manager leading a team developing a new product. Unfortunately, the latest version of your product fails the quality check. Since each version is developed based on the previous one, all the versions after a bad version are also bad.

Suppose you have n versions [1, 2, ..., n] and you want to find out the first bad one. You have access to a boolean API `is_bad_version(v)`. Implement a function that finds the first bad version, minimizing the number of API calls.

The harness calls `first_bad_version(n, first_bad)` and configures `is_bad_version` to return True for any v >= first_bad — your solution should only consult `is_bad_version`, not `first_bad` directly.
interviewerContext: First Bad Version. 1 <= bad <= n <= 2^31 - 1. Optimal: binary search on [1..n] using the API; O(log n) calls, O(1) space. Edge: bad == 1 (first one is bad), bad == n, n == 1. Common pitfall: low + high overflow in other languages (Python is fine). Watch: don't compare to `first_bad` directly — that's only for the simulated API.
starterCode:
# --- harness scaffolding (do not modify) ---
_FIRST_BAD = 0

def is_bad_version(v):
    return v >= _FIRST_BAD
# -------------------------------------------

def first_bad_version(n, first_bad):
    global _FIRST_BAD
    _FIRST_BAD = first_bad
    # TODO: binary search for the smallest v in [1..n] with is_bad_version(v) == True.
    pass

title: Linked List Cycle
candidateDescription:
Given the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it.

The harness builds the list from `values` and creates a cycle by pointing the tail's next to index `pos` (or no cycle if pos == -1). Return true if there is a cycle, false otherwise.
interviewerContext: Linked List Cycle (Floyd's tortoise and hare). 0 <= nodes <= 10^4. Optimal: two-pointer slow/fast, O(n) time, O(1) space. Hash-set approach is O(n) space and not what the interviewer wants. Edge: empty list, single node with self-loop, single node no loop, two nodes with/without loop. Common pitfall: not checking fast.next before dereferencing fast.next.next.

hiddenTestCases.description: cycle at the tail (self-loop on last)

title: Move Zeroes
candidateDescription:
Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. Return the modified array.

Note: ideally you would do this in-place without making a copy of the array.
interviewerContext: Move Zeroes. 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1. Optimal: two-pointer write-index, O(n) time, O(1) extra. One pass writes non-zeros forward, a second pass fills zeros — or single pass with swap. Edge: all zeros, no zeros, all the same value, single element. Common pitfall: changing the relative order of non-zeros while moving.

title: Same Tree
candidateDescription: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, return true if they are structurally identical and every corresponding node has the same value. Trees are passed as level-order arrays with null for missing children (LeetCode encoding).
interviewerContext: Same Tree. 0 <= nodes <= 100. Optimal: O(n) recursion comparing root values and recursing on left/left and right/right. BFS iterative with two queues also fine. Edge: both empty, one empty other not, same structure different values, same values different structure (left vs right child).

hiddenTestCases.description: deep identical trees with sparse children

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
candidateDescription: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
interviewerContext: Longest substring unique chars. s length up to 5 * 10^4. Optimal O(n) sliding window with last-seen map. Edge: empty string, all same char, spaces, full string unique.

hiddenTestCases.description: left pointer must not move backwards

followUps.prompt: Solid. Now generalize it: given a string and an integer k, return the length of the longest substring containing at most k distinct characters. Your sliding window is already close — walk me through the change.

title: Product of Array Except Self
candidateDescription: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer where answer[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i]. You must solve it without division and in O(n) time.
interviewerContext: Product except self. Length 2 to 10^5, nums can be negative or zero. Prefix/suffix products O(n), O(1) extra if output array not counted. Edge: zeros (multiple zeros), negatives.

title: Course Schedule
candidateDescription: You must take a total of num_courses courses, labeled from 0 to num_courses - 1. You are given an array prerequisites where prerequisites[j] = [aj, bj] means you must take course bj before course aj. Return true if you can finish all courses. Otherwise return false.
interviewerContext: Course Schedule (topological feasibility). 1 <= numCourses <= 2000, prerequisites.length <= 5000. Directed graph: edge b -> a means b before a. Return whether a valid order exists (no directed cycle). Optimal O(V+E) via Kahn (indegree/BFS) or DFS cycle detection. Edge: empty prerequisites, disconnected components, self-loop as cycle, multiple edges.

followUps.prompt: Nice. The follow-on is: return one valid ordering of all course numbers (a list of length num_courses) that respects every prerequisite, or an empty list if it is impossible. How would you adapt your approach?

title: 3Sum
candidateDescription: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] such that a + b + c == 0. Each triplet must be sorted in non-decreasing order, and the returned list must also be sorted in lexicographic order. The result must not contain duplicate triplets.
interviewerContext: 3Sum. 3 <= nums.length <= 3000, -10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5. Optimal: sort O(n log n) then for each i, two-pointer scan in O(n), total O(n^2). Dedup by skipping equal neighbours at i, lo, and hi. Edge: fewer than 3 elements (return []), all zeros, all positives or all negatives (no triplet sums to 0), many duplicates. Common pitfalls: forgetting to dedup, or O(n^3) brute force.

hiddenTestCases.description: duplicates resolve to a single triplet
many overlapping triplets — strong dedup test

title: Group Anagrams
candidateDescription:
Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together.

Return the groups in a deterministic order: sort each group lexicographically, then sort the list of groups by the first element of each group.
interviewerContext: Group Anagrams. 1 <= strs.length <= 10^4, 0 <= strs[i].length <= 100, lowercase. Optimal: O(N * K) using a 26-length character-count tuple as the key (K = avg word length). Sorting each word for the key is O(N * K log K). Edge: empty string is its own group, single string. Output ordering normalized for testability — interviewer should call out that real LC accepts any order. Common pitfall: using mutable list as a dict key.

hiddenTestCases.description: same chars, different counts — different groups

title: Top K Frequent Elements
candidateDescription:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements.

Return the answer sorted by frequency in descending order, breaking ties by value in ascending order. The result is guaranteed to be unique.
interviewerContext: Top K Frequent Elements. 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, k is in [1, number of unique elements]. Optimal: count frequencies O(n), then either bucket-sort by frequency O(n) or a min-heap of size k O(n log k). Sorting all is O(n log n). Edge: k equals number of distinct elements, all elements unique, all elements same. Output ordering normalized for testability (real LC accepts any).

hiddenTestCases.description: all unique, tie broken by value asc
ties — sort by value asc among ties

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
candidateDescription: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s. If multiple palindromes have the same maximum length, return the one whose starting index is smallest.
interviewerContext: Longest Palindromic Substring. 1 <= s.length <= 1000, mixed-case ASCII. Optimal interview answer: expand around centers, O(n^2) time, O(1) space — naturally returns the leftmost on ties. DP is also O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space. Manacher's is O(n) but rarely expected. Edge: single char (palindrome), all same char, no palindrome longer than 1, palindrome at the boundary. Output ordering: leftmost on ties.

hiddenTestCases.description: long even-length palindrome in the middle
whole string is an odd-length palindrome
whole string odd palindrome around center

title: Container With Most Water
candidateDescription: You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]). Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the most water. Return the maximum area.
interviewerContext: Container With Most Water. 2 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= height[i] <= 10^4. Optimal: two-pointer at both ends, move the shorter line inward, O(n) time, O(1) space. Brute force is O(n^2). Edge: two lines, equal heights, monotonic heights, zeros. Common pitfall: moving the taller pointer (gives strictly non-better areas).

hiddenTestCases.description: equal heights at ends — full width
small array, peak in the middle
ends matter even when interior is taller

title: Number of Islands
candidateDescription:
Given an m x n 2D grid of integers where 1 represents land and 0 represents water, return the number of islands.

An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.
interviewerContext: Number of Islands. 1 <= m, n <= 300. Optimal: DFS or BFS flood fill, O(m*n) time, O(m*n) worst-case stack/queue. Union-Find also works and is what some interviewers ask in follow-up. Edge: empty grid, single cell (land or water), grid all land (one island), grid all water (zero), diagonal connections do NOT form an island. Common pitfall: mutating input grid without flagging (often acceptable but mention it).

followUps.prompt: Nice. Now imagine the grid is being streamed in and you're told 'land cell created at (r,c)' one at a time. After each update, return the current number of islands. What data structure do you reach for?

title: Rotting Oranges
candidateDescription:
You are given an m x n grid where each cell can have one of three values:
- 0 representing an empty cell
- 1 representing a fresh orange
- 2 representing a rotten orange

Every minute, any fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes that must elapse until no cell has a fresh orange. If this is impossible, return -1.
interviewerContext: Rotting Oranges. 1 <= m, n <= 10. Multi-source BFS — seed queue with all rotten cells, BFS in layers, count minutes. Track remaining fresh count; if > 0 after BFS, return -1. O(m*n). Edge: no fresh oranges (return 0), no rotten oranges but fresh exist (return -1), grid all empty, grid all rotten. Common pitfall: incrementing minutes when a layer rots nothing (off-by-one).

hiddenTestCases.description: fresh isolated from rotten by an empty row

title: Coin Change
candidateDescription: You are given an integer array coins representing coins of different denominations and an integer amount representing a total amount of money. Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. If that amount cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return -1. You may assume an infinite number of each kind of coin.
interviewerContext: Coin Change. 1 <= coins.length <= 12, 1 <= coins[i] <= 2^31 - 1, 0 <= amount <= 10^4. Optimal: bottom-up DP, dp[a] = min coins for amount a, O(amount * coins). Greedy is WRONG (e.g. coins [1,3,4], amount 6 — greedy 4+1+1=3, DP 3+3=2). Edge: amount=0 → 0 coins, amount<smallest coin → -1, amount achievable only via large denominations. Common pitfall: initializing dp[0] incorrectly.

title: House Robber
candidateDescription:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. The only constraint stopping you is that adjacent houses have a connected security system, and contacting the police will be triggered if two adjacent houses are broken into on the same night.

Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.
interviewerContext: House Robber. 1 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 400. Optimal: O(n) DP with two rolling vars, O(1) space. Recurrence: rob(i) = max(rob(i-1), rob(i-2) + nums[i]). Edge: empty (return 0), one house, two houses (pick max), all zeros. Common pitfall: forgetting that adjacency constraint allows skipping more than one (always take the better of skip-one vs take-current).

hiddenTestCases.description: best is the two ends, equal interior

followUps.prompt: Good. Now suppose the houses are arranged in a circle — the first and last houses are also adjacent. How does that change your DP?

title: Word Break
candidateDescription: Given a string s and a dictionary of strings word_dict, return true if s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. The same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times in the segmentation.
interviewerContext: Word Break. 1 <= s.length <= 300, 1 <= word_dict.length <= 1000. Optimal: O(n^2) DP with a set of words — dp[i] is True if s[:i] is segmentable. Substring check is O(L) where L is max word length, so total O(n * n * L) worst case; in practice with hashing of dictionary it's effectively O(n^2). BFS / Memoized DFS also fine. Edge: empty dict (False unless s is empty), word longer than s, repeated words, s itself is one word.

hiddenTestCases.description: almost fits but trailing 'b' breaks it

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
candidateDescription: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time.
interviewerContext: Longest Consecutive Sequence. 0 <= nums.length <= 10^5. Optimal: O(n) — put all nums in a set, for each x that is the START of a run (i.e. x-1 not in set) walk forward counting. Sorting is O(n log n) and disqualified by the constraint. Edge: empty array (0), all duplicates (1), single element (1), very long single run, two disjoint runs. Common pitfall: starting a walk from every number — that's O(n^2) without the 'is start' check.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
candidateDescription:
Given the root of a binary tree (provided as a level-order array with null for missing children), determine if it is a valid binary search tree.

A valid BST is defined as follows: every node's value is strictly greater than all values in its left subtree and strictly less than all values in its right subtree.
interviewerContext: Validate BST. 1 <= nodes <= 10^4, -2^31 <= node.val <= 2^31 - 1. Optimal: recursive with (low, high) bounds, O(n) time, O(h) stack. Alternative: in-order traversal must be strictly increasing. Edge: single node (valid), duplicate values (invalid — strict), values at int boundaries, fully left chain. Common pitfall: only comparing parent to immediate child without propagating bounds (e.g. [5,1,4,null,null,3,6] looks fine at each parent-child but 3 < 5).

hiddenTestCases.description: violation deeper — 6 < 10 but in right subtree
extreme bounds — beware naive infinity sentinels

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
candidateDescription: Given the root of a binary tree (passed as a level-order array with null for missing children), return the level order traversal of its nodes' values — a list of lists, where each inner list contains the values at that depth, in left-to-right order.
interviewerContext: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal. 0 <= nodes <= 2000. Optimal: BFS with a queue, capture queue size at start of each level, O(n) time, O(w) queue (w = max width). DFS with depth-keyed buckets also works. Edge: empty tree → [], single node → [[v]], left-skewed chain (one node per level), right-skewed chain. Common pitfall: not capturing the level size before draining.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
candidateDescription: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. Note that it is the kth largest element in sorted order, not the kth distinct element.
interviewerContext: Kth Largest. 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4. Common interview answers: min-heap of size k → O(n log k); quickselect → O(n) average, O(n^2) worst (Hoare partition, random pivot to mitigate). Sort + index is O(n log n). Edge: k == 1 (max), k == n (min), duplicates (kth in sorted order counts duplicates), all same. Common pitfall: confusing kth largest with kth distinct.

hiddenTestCases.description: all negative, k=1 is the max

title: Merge Intervals
candidateDescription: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. The returned intervals must be sorted by start.
interviewerContext: Merge Intervals. 1 <= intervals.length <= 10^4. Optimal: sort by start O(n log n), then sweep — extend the last interval's end if the next start <= last end. O(n log n) total. Edge: single interval, all disjoint, all overlapping (one merged), touching intervals like [1,4][4,5] (treat as overlapping). Common pitfall: assuming input is sorted; not handling end-equals-next-start.

hiddenTestCases.description: one big interval swallows the rest

title: Insert Interval
candidateDescription: You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i] sorted by start_i, and a new_interval [start, end]. Insert new_interval into intervals such that the result is still sorted in ascending order by start_i and intervals still do not have any overlapping (merging if necessary). Return the result.
interviewerContext: Insert Interval. 0 <= intervals.length <= 10^4. Optimal: O(n) single pass — add all intervals ending before new_interval starts, merge all intervals overlapping new_interval, append all intervals starting after merged end. Edge: empty input (return [new]), new_interval before everything, new_interval after everything, new_interval swallows several, new_interval inside an existing interval. Common pitfall: using binary search + sort O(n log n) when a single linear pass suffices.

hiddenTestCases.description: new sits cleanly between two existing intervals

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
candidateDescription: There is an integer array nums sorted in ascending order with distinct values. Prior to being passed to your function, nums is possibly rotated at an unknown pivot index k. Given the array and a target integer, return the index of target if it is in nums, or -1 if it is not. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime.
interviewerContext: Search in Rotated Sorted Array. 1 <= nums.length <= 5000, all unique. Optimal: modified binary search — at each step decide which half is sorted (left half sorted iff nums[low] <= nums[mid]) and recurse into whichever sorted half could contain target. O(log n). Edge: not rotated (k=0), single element, target absent, target at pivot. Common pitfall: missing the case where nums[low] == nums[mid] when duplicates exist (irrelevant here since distinct, but mention).

hiddenTestCases.description: small array, target in right sorted half
target at index 1 in rotated array

title: Word Search
candidateDescription:
Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word exists in the grid.

The word can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same letter cell may not be used more than once.
interviewerContext: Word Search. 1 <= m, n <= 6, 1 <= word.length <= 15. Optimal: DFS with backtracking — for each starting cell matching word[0], recurse 4-way marking visited via temporary character mutation or visited set, O(m*n * 4^L) worst case. Edge: word longer than total cells (False), single-cell board, repeated chars in word causing self-visit. Common pitfall: forgetting to restore the cell on backtrack.

title: Permutations
candidateDescription:
Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations.

Return the permutations in lexicographic order (sort the final list of lists).
interviewerContext: Permutations. 1 <= nums.length <= 6. Optimal: backtracking, O(n * n!) time. Approach: either build via swap-in-place or via a 'used' set. Edge: single element, two elements. Output ordering normalized to lex sort. Common pitfall: producing duplicates (not an issue here since input is distinct; mention it for the dup variant).

title: Spiral Matrix
candidateDescription: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order, starting from the top-left corner and proceeding clockwise.
interviewerContext: Spiral Matrix. 1 <= m, n <= 10. Optimal: maintain four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and walk each side, shrinking after, O(m*n) time. Direction-vector simulation also works. Edge: 1xN row, Nx1 column, single cell, non-square matrices (m != n), even/odd dimensions. Common pitfall: double-visiting the last row/column when only one row or column remains.

title: Jump Game
candidateDescription: You are given an integer array nums. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position. Return true if you can reach the last index, or false otherwise.
interviewerContext: Jump Game. 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5. Optimal: greedy — track farthest reachable index, return False if i > farthest at any step, else True if farthest >= n-1. O(n) time, O(1) space. DP O(n^2) also works. Edge: single element (True), starts with 0 but has length > 1 (False), all zeros after start, exact reach. Common pitfall: greedy from the back is also valid but harder to explain.

hiddenTestCases.description: single element — already at the end
skip past zeros via larger jump

title: Daily Temperatures
candidateDescription: Given an array of integers temperatures representing the daily temperatures, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after the ith day to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future day for which this is possible, answer[i] should be 0.
interviewerContext: Daily Temperatures. 1 <= n <= 10^5. Optimal: monotonic decreasing stack of indices, O(n) time, O(n) stack. Brute force O(n^2).
